At Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital, run by the government, a clinical social worker sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings (£2,000), using real transfer paperwork. The reporters took all the children to a children's home. When the story ran in November 2020, the official appeared to still have his job and the clinic appeared to still be operating.

On the coast, a 2006 study by UNICEF and the Kenyan government found that Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of the clients of exploited children, and Kenyans 38 per cent. The 2025 US trafficking report cites a 2023 study estimating more than 2,000 children exploited in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and holiday homes rather than hotels. It also describes rings moving girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and notes concerns about officials taking part, with no action reported against them. Some foreign offenders are prosecuted at home: Keith Morris was jailed in the UK for 18.5 years for offences against children in Kenya, one of about eight UK prosecutions for offences abroad since 1997.

Kenya is also the setting of a false accusation. In May 2011 the Irish broadcaster RTÉ's documentary "Mission to Prey" said an Irish priest, Fr Kevin Reynolds, had fathered a child with a minor in Kenya. It was untrue. RTÉ apologised, paid him a large libel settlement, and its director general called it one of its gravest mistakes.

For a novice: the trade in Kenya moved from hotels to private villas, and in one hospital it used official forms. A false story, like RTÉ's, can make real cases harder to believe. When reading a report, ask whether it was tested, and whether the officials it names were ever investigated.

patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. previous_draft:
In 1964, in Lima, a Spanish Jesuit named Alfonso Pedrajas abused a minor for the first time. He then settled in neighbouring Bolivia, where he abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools. In 1978 he confessed to a superior, who covered it up. Peru has also been on the receiving end of the same kind of move: in 2010 a Marist Brother in Chile, Abel Pérez, confessed to his superiors that he had abused minors, and the Marist Brothers transferred him to Peru.

Peru's main reckoning so far came from inside a Catholic movement rather than from the state. In 2016 the Catholic movement Sodalitium Christianae Vitae commissioned an inquiry into its founder, Luis Figari. Its report, in February 2017, found that he had sexually abused at least one minor and others.

Today the visible exploitation is tied to tourism and to mining and logging. The 2025 US trafficking report says tourists from the United States and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Peruvian Amazon. In Loreto, criminal groups take foreign tourists by boat to remote places on the Amazon River where women and children are exploited. Peruvian, Venezuelan and Bolivian women and girls are lured to mining and logging camps, and the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua has reportedly moved trafficking victims from the Colombian border city of Cúcuta to Peru. Peruvian courts convicted 59 traffickers in 2024. Two police officers were charged with crimes against trafficking victims, and the report says corruption remained a significant concern. Peru also sends children abroad for adoption: 2,049 between 2003 and 2022.

For a novice: Peru shows abusers being moved across borders by religious orders in both directions, and an inquiry paid for by the movement whose founder was accused. When a church body investigates itself, ask who chose the investigators and whether police were told. In remote river and mining areas, ask who is there to check on children.

Since war broke out in Sudan in 2023, an independent UN fact-finding mission has collected accounts from women and girls across the country. It found rape and gang rape were widespread, carried out mostly by men in the uniform of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias, with some cases by the Sudanese Armed Forces. The victims included girls as young as 8. The mission found that the RSF's abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes amounted to sexual slavery. The UN Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023, 57 of them by the RSF, and against 74 children in 2024, 54 by the RSF and 9 by militia linked to it. The UN now lists the RSF for the rape and abduction of children. Soldiers from a neighbouring country appear in the same records: the UN attributed 4 of 35 verified cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan to Chad's national army.

Sudan is also a destination. The 2025 US trafficking report says Ethiopian girls are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes kept under control with drugs, and that reports of officials taking part continued.

These UN counts are what has been verified in a war zone, not the total. The Middle East and North Africa region has no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children, so that side is not counted at all.

For a novice: in Sudan the main abusers named by the UN are armed forces, the same groups that hold power over the territory where the children live. When you see a verified number such as 114 girls, ask how many cases the UN could not reach, and which court, if any, can try a commander for it.
